title: Building Effective Organizations
question: How should an organization divide work, assign decisions and measure performance so that capable people accomplish more together than they could alone?

overview.text: Organizations exist because some work is too large, too specialized or too continuous for individuals acting alone. That advantage has a price. Once work is divided, someone must decide who does what, who decides what, how information moves, and how anyone knows whether it is working. This week treats organization design as a set of choices with predictable trade-offs, not a matter of taste, fashion or the latest reorganization.

You will move from the field’s founding ideas—differentiation and integration, the information-processing view, Mintzberg’s configurations and the arithmetic of spans and layers—to decision rights and the economics of delegation, then to the strongest modern evidence that management practices matter, including a randomized experiment and its long-run follow-up. The week ends below the chart, with routines, culture and team design: the parts of an organization that carry its knowledge and resist change.

Keep two disciplines from earlier weeks in view. From [Week 4](#w04): ask what kind of evidence supports each claim—theory, comparative study, survey correlation or experiment. From [Week 6](#w06): remember that formal design competes with informal power. The Organization Builder lets you feel the trade-offs under a budget that does not stretch far enough; the hospital case asks you to apply them where money and people’s working lives are both at stake; and the assignment asks you to design and defend a department of your own.

objectives: Explain how differentiation, integration and information-processing load determine which structure fits a task and its environment.
Allocate decision rights by locating specific knowledge and weighing agency costs, and record them with a labelled practitioner tool.
Evaluate the evidence that management practices cause performance, distinguishing correlational, experimental and long-run findings.
Diagnose metric gaming with Goodhart’s law and the multitask incentive problem, and design countermeasures within an operating rhythm.
Design a department—roles, spans, decision rights, coordination mechanisms, operating rhythm and metrics—and defend the trade-offs it accepts.

lessons.title: Why Structure Exists: Differentiation, Integration and Information Load
lessons.summary: Structure is a bet about where information and coordination problems will arise; good designs match differentiation, integration, spans and layers to the uncertainty of the work.
objectives: Explain differentiation and integration and why effective organizations need both in the degree their environment demands.
Use the information-processing view to choose among slack resources, self-contained units, vertical information systems and lateral relations.
Match coordinating mechanisms to types of work, and calculate how span of control changes layers and management cost.
lessons.executive: An organization chart is not a picture of status; it is a theory about which conversations matter most. Every structure divides work so specialists can go deep (differentiation) and then pays to reconnect them (integration). Contingency theory and the information-processing view give a practical test: the more uncertain the work, the more exceptions it throws up, and the sooner a hierarchy alone will choke. You can respond by reducing the information load—slack, self-contained units—or by raising capacity—better information systems, lateral roles. Spans and layers are the cost side of that choice. Before any reorganization, ask what information problem the new chart solves and which working routines it will break.

explore.text: Picture two regional banks that decide, in the same year, to merge their fraud-detection team and their credit-underwriting team into one “risk analytics” unit. The logic sounds unanswerable: both teams build models on customer data, both report to the chief risk officer, and both complain that the other hoards data. One bank’s merged unit thrives. The other loses its best fraud analysts within a year, and fraud losses climb. The banks are hypothetical, but the pattern is familiar to anyone who has lived through a reorganization: identical boxes on a chart, opposite results.

The difference usually lies in something the chart does not show. Fraud work runs on minutes: an attack begins on a Saturday night and someone must change a rule before Sunday morning. Credit work runs on quarters: a cutoff change is tested, documented, reviewed and defended to regulators. The two teams do not merely sit in different rooms; they live on different clocks, answer to different definitions of a good outcome and need different kinds of supervision. Merging them can let them share data and talent, or it can force one rhythm onto work that needs another.

Before reading on: when two units are merged to improve coordination, list two things the merged organization gains and two it can lose. Which of the losses would show up on a dashboard, and which would not?

This lesson gives you the vocabulary to answer that question with more than intuition. It starts from the oldest problem in organization design—how to divide work and then put it back together—and ends with the arithmetic of spans and layers, which turns abstract design choices into headcount and cost.

understand.text: Two opposing forces

Paul Lawrence and Jay Lorsch framed organization design as a tension between two forces. *Differentiation* is the degree to which subunits develop different goals, time horizons, interpersonal styles and degrees of formal structure as each adapts to its own part of the environment. *Integration* is the quality of collaboration among those subunits that the organization needs to achieve unity of effort. Comparing organizations that operated in the same industrial environment, they reached a conclusion that still surprises managers: the more effective organizations were not the least differentiated. They achieved both the differentiation their environment demanded and the integration needed to hold it together. And because differentiated units see the world differently, the more differentiation an organization needs, the harder and more deliberate its integration must be.

This is the core of *contingency theory*: there is no single best structure, only structures that fit or misfit their task and environment. Fit is not a matter of taste. A structure fits when it supplies the coordination the work actually requires at a cost the organization can bear.
Structure as an information-processing system

Jay Galbraith sharpened the idea by treating organizations as information-processing systems. His starting proposition is that the greater the uncertainty of a task, the more information must be processed among decision-makers while the task is being done. Routine work can be coordinated by rules and programs, by referring exceptions up the hierarchy, and by setting targets that leave the method to the people doing the work. As uncertainty rises, exceptions multiply and the hierarchy overloads: managers become the bottleneck through which every unusual case must pass.

Galbraith described two families of response. An organization can *reduce the need* for information processing, by creating slack resources (longer lead times, spare capacity, buffers, less demanding targets) or by creating self-contained units that hold every skill a product, customer or region needs. Or it can *increase its capacity* to process information, by investing in vertical information systems that move better data up and down faster, or by creating lateral relations—direct contact, liaison roles, task forces, teams, integrating roles and, at the extreme, matrix structures—that let decisions be made across units without climbing the hierarchy. Each strategy has a cost; choosing none of them means accepting lower performance by default.

understand.text: Five ways to coordinate

Henry Mintzberg synthesized the research on structure into five coordinating mechanisms: direct supervision (one person instructs others), standardization of work processes (the method is specified), standardization of outputs (the result is specified), standardization of skills (the training is specified, so trained people can coordinate almost automatically) and mutual adjustment (people coordinate through informal communication). He argued that organizations cluster into five configurations, each dominated by one mechanism and pulled by one part of the organization.

understand.text: The configurations are ideal types, not boxes that real organizations fit neatly. Their value lies in the diagnostic question they force: which coordinating mechanism is actually doing the work here, and is it the right one for this task? A professional bureaucracy that tries to coordinate surgeons through detailed process scripts will meet resistance, because the professionals already coordinate through shared training. An adhocracy that drifts into standard procedures will lose the improvisation it exists to produce.
Spans, layers and the cost of control

*Span of control* is the number of people who report directly to one manager. It is where design meets arithmetic. Wider spans mean fewer managers and fewer layers, so information passes through fewer filters and decisions are made closer to the work. Narrower spans mean more coaching time per person and closer supervision, at the price of more managers and more layers. There is no research-backed universal number. The right span depends on how similar and standardized the work is, how expert the reports are, how much of the manager’s own time goes to non-supervisory work, how dispersed the team is and how much development each person needs.

That is why delayering appeals to finance teams. It is also why it is risky: every manager removed was absorbing exceptions, coaching people and translating between levels. If rules, information systems and lateral links do not absorb that load, the remaining managers become Galbraith’s bottleneck.

blocks.text: A solid line on a chart usually means formal authority: the manager can assign work, evaluate performance and influence pay. A dotted line usually means a second, advisory relationship—someone whose input matters but who does not control the person’s job. Three basic structures recur. A *functional* structure groups people by expertise (all engineers together, all nurses together); it builds depth but makes cross-functional work slow. A *divisional* structure groups people by product, customer or region; it speeds work within each division but duplicates specialists. A *matrix* gives people two bosses, one functional and one divisional, to capture both benefits; it works only when the organization can handle the conflict it deliberately builds in.
When you read any chart, ask three questions: who can say yes, who can say no, and whose phone rings when something unusual happens.

understand.title: Methodological note: what contingency research can and cannot show

blocks.text: Contingency theory makes a causal claim—fit between structure and environment improves performance—from evidence that is mostly comparative and cross-sectional. Lawrence and Lorsch compared a small number of organizations at one point in time. Studies of this kind are excellent for generating hypotheses and weak at ruling out alternatives: a better-managed firm may achieve both differentiation and integration because it is better managed, not because fit causes success.

A second problem is circularity. If fit is defined after the fact as whatever the successful organizations did, the theory cannot fail. A testable version must define the required differentiation and integration in advance—for example, from measurable uncertainty in the task—and then predict which organizations will struggle. When anyone tells you a structure “fits” your strategy, ask what observation would have shown that it did not.

challenge.text: Three objections deserve a hearing. First, the information-processing view treats people as channels and decisions as data transfers. Real organizations are also political systems. A structure that routes information efficiently may still fail if it strips a powerful group of status or control; [Week 6](#w06-l1) examined how informal authority reshapes formal design. Second, ideal types tempt leaders to copy a configuration rather than diagnose their own work. Most organizations are hybrids: a hospital is a professional bureaucracy in the operating room, a machine bureaucracy in billing and an adhocracy in its innovation unit.

Third, structure may matter less than executives believe. Reorganizations are visible, quick to announce and easy to attribute to a new leader, which makes them attractive whether or not they solve the underlying problem. APERTURE’s working hypothesis—not an established finding—is that many reorganizations change the chart while leaving the real coordination problem untouched (unclear decision rights, missing information, weak routines), and impose a transition cost by breaking the informal routines people had built ([Lesson 4](#w08-l4)). Treat claims that delayering or reorganizing improves performance as hypotheses to test in your setting, not as general laws.

There is also a competing account of why structure matters: incentives rather than information. A self-contained unit can be measured on its own results, which sharpens accountability but encourages it to optimize locally at the expense of the whole. A matrix blurs accountability precisely because it shares it. The next two lessons take up that thread—who holds decision rights, and how measures and rewards change behavior.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the reorganization you inherit

blocks.text: You join an organization six months after a reorganization. Morale is low, two respected people have left, and the chief operating officer asks whether to reverse it. No one measured performance before the change, so you cannot compare. Reversing it would be a second disruption; keeping it may lock in a mistake. A defensible first move is diagnostic rather than structural: identify the three or four recurring decisions and hand-offs that matter most, trace how each worked before and how it works now, and ask which coordinating mechanism was lost. Often the answer is a specific routine or integrating role that can be restored without undoing the whole design.

apply.text: Consider a hypothetical 400-bed hospital whose emergency department and elective surgery service fight constantly over beds. The emergency department lives on a minute-to-minute clock and values speed; surgery plans weeks ahead and values predictability. Differentiation is appropriate—each unit should be good at its own work—but integration is failing. Galbraith’s menu clarifies the options. Slack: hold a small number of beds in reserve, accepting idle cost. Self-contained units: give surgery its own dedicated recovery ward, accepting duplication. Vertical information: a real-time bed board visible to both, accepting systems cost. Lateral relations: a bed-management coordinator with authority to arbitrate in real time, accepting a new role and some conflict. A thoughtful leader usually combines two of these and is explicit about the cost of each.

The same diagnosis travels. A hypothetical consulting firm whose industry practices and functional practices compete for the same partners faces differentiation between client knowledge and technical depth; it often responds with a matrix and staffing coordinators. A government agency that must align field offices with a central policy unit faces differentiation in time horizon and formality; liaison roles and standardized reporting are its usual answers. A professional soccer club’s first-team staff and academy differ in horizon and in what counts as success; a technical director often serves as the integrating role.

In player development, differentiation is built in. Field coaches work on a daily clock and value relationships and feel; analysts work on longer horizons and value measurement; performance science and medical staff answer to health standards that are not negotiable; international operations work across languages, distances and legal systems. The design question is not how to erase those differences but how much integration the work requires and which mechanism supplies it: a coordinator role that spans field and analytics, standardized individual plans that carry information between levels, a short daily huddle, or a shared information system. Each choice costs people, time or autonomy. Naming the information problem first keeps you from buying the wrong mechanism.

retain.text: Structure divides work so specialists can go deep, and then spends money and attention to reconnect them. The uncertainty of the work sets how much reconnecting is needed; Galbraith’s four strategies, Mintzberg’s five mechanisms and the arithmetic of spans tell you how to supply it and what it will cost. Fit is a hypothesis to test, not a label to award after the fact.
Name the two units in your own organization that are most differentiated. What integrating mechanism connects them today, and what does it cost?
Using Galbraith’s menu, which strategy would you try first for a team drowning in escalations, and why?
Without looking back, explain why moving from a span of five to a span of twelve can be both a saving and a risk.

takeaways: Every structure trades the depth that differentiation buys against the cost of integration; effective organizations achieve both in the degree their work requires.
Task uncertainty drives information load: when exceptions overwhelm the hierarchy, reduce the load (slack, self-contained units) or raise capacity (information systems, lateral relations).
Mintzberg’s configurations are diagnostic ideal types—identify which coordinating mechanism actually does the work.
Span of control is arithmetic with consequences: wider spans remove layers and cost, and also remove exception-handling and coaching capacity.

check.prompt: A software company’s product teams escalate dozens of cross-team dependencies to the chief technology officer every week, and releases stall. In Galbraith’s terms, which response *increases information-processing capacity* rather than reducing the need for it?

Give each product team its own platform engineers so most dependencies disappear
Create a cross-team integration role with authority to resolve dependency conflicts directly
Lower release targets so fewer features compete for shared engineers

check.explanation: An integrating role is a lateral relation: it adds capacity to make cross-unit decisions without sending every exception up the hierarchy. Longer cycles and lower targets are slack, and dedicated engineers create self-contained units; both of those reduce the need for information processing instead of increasing capacity. All four are legitimate strategies—the question asks you to classify, not to rank them.

optionFeedback.a: Longer cycles are slack resources: they reduce the information load by loosening time pressure rather than adding capacity.
optionFeedback.b: Dedicated engineers make each team more self-contained, which reduces the need for coordination rather than increasing capacity to handle it.
optionFeedback.d: Lower targets are another form of slack; they shrink the coordination problem instead of adding capacity to solve it.

lessons.title: Who Decides? Decision Rights, Knowledge and Coordination
lessons.summary: Decision rights should sit where the relevant knowledge is cheapest to find, but every move toward the knowledge raises agency costs, so rights, measures and rewards must be designed as one system.
objectives: Distinguish specific from general knowledge and use the distinction to locate decision rights.
Weigh the costs of centralizing and decentralizing particular decisions, and pair any delegation with measurement and accountability.
Use RACI or RAPID as labelled practitioner tools, and evaluate Conway’s law as an observation with mixed evidence.
lessons.executive: Many coordination failures that leaders call “communication problems” are decision-rights problems: nobody knows who decides, or three people think they do. Jensen and Meckling’s rule of thumb is to put a decision where the knowledge it needs is cheapest to find—often close to the work—while recognizing that the person holding that knowledge may not share the organization’s goals. Delegation therefore comes bundled with measurement and rewards; one without the others fails. Practitioner tools such as RACI and RAPID help you write the answer down, but they do not supply the answer. And remember Conway’s observation: what you build will tend to mirror how your teams communicate, unless shared standards and tools break the mirror.

explore.text: A hypothetical national retail bank lets branch managers approve small-business loans up to a set limit. Branch managers know things no model captures: that the bakery owner has run three businesses successfully, that the new shopping strip is half empty, that a borrower’s partner just left the business. Losses on branch-approved loans are low. Then a new chief credit officer centralizes approval in a head-office team using a scoring model, citing inconsistency and two fraud cases. Approval times triple, branch managers stop sending their best prospects, and the small-business portfolio shrinks. Two years later, a different executive decentralizes again—and loses money on a wave of loans approved by branch managers who are paid on volume.

Neither executive was foolish. Each saw half of a real trade-off. The first saw that branch managers held knowledge the center could not cheaply obtain. The second saw that people paid on volume will not always use that knowledge in the bank’s interest. The design problem is to get both halves right at once, and it is the same problem whether the decision is a loan, a hospital discharge, a software release or a player’s promotion.
Before reading on: for one recurring decision in your work, write down who actually makes it, who believes they make it, and who holds the information that matters most. Are they the same person?

understand.text: Specific and general knowledge

Michael Jensen and William Meckling built a theory of organizational structure on a distinction between two kinds of knowledge. *General knowledge* is cheap to transmit: prices, volumes, a model score, a regulation. *Specific knowledge* is costly to transmit: it is tacit, perishable or local, like a nurse’s sense that a patient is deteriorating before the vital signs show it, or a branch manager’s read of a borrower. Because specific knowledge is expensive to move to the decision-maker, organizations face a choice: move the knowledge up to where the decision rights are, or move the decision rights down to where the knowledge is.

Moving rights down reduces the cost of decisions made with poor information. But it raises a second cost: the people now holding the rights have their own interests, and the organization must spend on monitoring, measurement and incentives to keep their decisions aligned—agency costs. Jensen and Meckling’s picture is a trade-off: as decision rights move lower, information costs fall and agency costs rise, and the best level is the one that minimizes their sum. That is why they treated structure as interlocking systems that must be designed together: the assignment of decision rights, the system for measuring performance, and the system for rewarding and punishing.

understand.text: Centralization versus decentralization

With that frame, the familiar debate becomes a list of specific trade-offs rather than a matter of philosophy. Centralization buys consistency, economies of scale, concentrated expertise, coordination across units and protection against local self-interest. Decentralization buys speed, local adaptation, use of specific knowledge and the motivation that comes from owning a decision. Every organization centralizes some decisions and decentralizes others; the skill lies in sorting decisions, not in choosing a side. Galbraith’s self-contained units from [Lesson 1](#w08-l1) are one form of decentralization: they move decisions to where the work is by giving each unit everything it needs.

understand.text: Writing decision rights down: practitioner tools

Two practitioner tools help organizations record who does what in a decision. They are heuristics from management practice, not research findings, and their value depends on the conversation they force rather than the grid they produce. *RACI* assigns, for each task or decision, who is Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the outcome and signs off—ideally exactly one person), Consulted (gives input beforehand) and Informed (told afterward). *RAPID*, a framework that originated in management consulting, focuses on decisions rather than tasks: who Recommends, who must Agree (a formal veto, to be used sparingly), who Performs the decision once made, who gives Input, and the one person who Decides.

understand.text: Conway’s observation

In 1968 a programmer, Melvin Conway, observed that organizations which design systems tend to produce designs that mirror their own communication structures. Researchers later restated the idea as the *mirroring hypothesis*: the ties among people and units in a project or firm will correspond to the technical dependencies in the work. Lyra Colfer and Carliss Baldwin reviewed 142 empirical studies and found mirroring common but not universal across industries and firms. The main exceptions came from open collaborative projects, mostly in software, where distributed contributors coordinated through shared code, documentation and tools rather than organizational ties.

Treat Conway’s law as an observation and a design heuristic, not a law of nature. Its practical use is diagnostic: if a hospital’s patient record is fragmented along department lines, or a company’s product feels like three products stitched together, look at how the teams that built it communicate. Its practitioner corollary—sometimes called the “inverse Conway maneuver”—is to organize teams around the architecture you want. The review’s exceptions are the warning: when coordination can travel through shared standards and transparent tools, the mirror can be broken.

understand.title: Prerequisite: the principal–agent problem in one paragraph

blocks.text: A *principal* (an owner, a board, a manager) delegates a decision or task to an *agent* (an executive, an employee, a contractor) whose interests are not identical and whose effort or information the principal cannot fully observe. The agent may shirk, take too much or too little risk, or pursue private goals. *Agency costs* are the sum of what the principal spends on monitoring and incentives, what the agent spends to reassure the principal, and the value lost when decisions still diverge. [Week 7](#w07-l4) met the idea in negotiation; here it explains why delegation is never free.

understand.title: Methodological note: why the decision-rights trade-off is hard to test

blocks.text: Jensen and Meckling’s argument is theory, built from first principles rather than from data. Testing it is difficult because organizations choose how much to decentralize, and they choose in response to the same unobserved conditions—competition, trust, the quality of their managers—that affect performance. A raw correlation between decentralization and performance therefore says little about what would happen if a given firm decentralized. Credible evidence comes from settings where the allocation of decision rights changes for reasons unrelated to performance, or from careful within-organization comparisons over time. When someone tells you that “empowered” organizations outperform, ask how the empowered organizations came to be empowered.

challenge.text: Four limits matter. First, decision-rights theory assumes that formal rights are the rights that matter. In practice, informal power often overrides the chart: the person who controls a key relationship or a scarce resource may hold an effective veto that appears in no grid. Writing rights down helps only if powerful people accept them; [Week 6](#w06-l1) explained why they may not.

Second, decentralization has costs that do not appear in the information–agency trade-off. Local discretion produces unequal treatment, which can become a fairness or legal problem in hiring, lending or clinical care. It can also fragment learning: ten units each solving the same problem in different ways learn more slowly than one that pools its experience. Third, crises pull decisions toward the center—sometimes appropriately, for speed and coordination, and sometimes because anxious leaders want control. An organization that has never practiced decentralized decisions will not perform them well on the day the center is overwhelmed.

Fourth, tools like RACI and RAPID can become theater. A grid that lists eleven Consulted parties for a routine decision documents a coordination problem without solving it. A useful test: for each recurring decision, could a new employee identify the one person who decides within a minute? If not, the grid is decoration. And the Conway evidence cuts in both directions: mirroring is common enough to take seriously and broken often enough that reorganizing teams is neither necessary nor sufficient to change what they build.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the decision nobody owns

blocks.text: Your product team wants to launch a feature that lets customers move money instantly. The fraud team says it will raise losses; the growth team says delay will cost the quarter. The decision sits between two vice presidents, each believing the other must sign off. You have 48 hours, partial loss estimates and no agreed decision owner. You cannot redesign the organization before Thursday. What you can do is name, for this decision only, one person who Decides, who Recommends, whose Input is required and whether anyone holds a veto—and write down what evidence after launch would trigger a reversal. A temporary, explicit allocation beats a permanent, implicit one, and it gives you a case to argue for a standing rule afterward.

apply.text: Consider a hypothetical consulting firm deciding how to staff engagements. Partners hold specific knowledge about clients; a central staffing team holds general knowledge about everyone’s availability and development needs. Fully decentralized staffing lets partners hoard stars and starve junior development; fully centralized staffing ignores client fit. A workable allocation: the staffing team Recommends, the engagement partner gives Input on client fit, the practice leader Decides contested cases, and the consultant is Informed early enough to raise concerns. The control system follows: partners are evaluated partly on the development of the people they staff, which reduces the incentive to hoard.

Apply the same logic to a player development department and the decision to move a player between levels. Field staff hold specific knowledge about readiness and how the player handles adversity; analysts hold knowledge from performance data; medical and performance staff hold knowledge about health and workload; the department head holds organizational context such as roster needs and other players’ timelines. One defensible allocation: the coordinator for that position group Recommends after a structured meeting; analysts, performance staff and current coaches give Input; medical staff hold an Agree right limited to health clearance, not performance judgment; the department head Decides; and the receiving coaches are Informed, with the player’s plan, before he arrives. The choices worth debating are where the veto stops and who decides when the head is unavailable.

Centralize or decentralize decision by decision, using knowledge, consistency, speed, interdependence and alignment as signals. Decision rights, performance measures and rewards are one system—change one and the others must change too.
Sort decisions one by one: knowledge location, cost of inconsistency, speed, interdependence and alignment decide which to centralize.
RACI and RAPID are practitioner heuristics for recording decisions; Conway’s law is an observation that holds often, not always.

Clinicians’ interests are perfectly aligned with the hospital’s, so agency costs are zero
Centralized decisions are always slower and therefore always worse
General knowledge such as bed counts should never influence clinical decisions

check.explanation: The framework places decision rights near specific knowledge when moving that knowledge is costly, as with tacit clinical judgment about readiness. It does not assume perfect alignment; agency costs still exist and are managed through measurement and review. General capacity information remains relevant and can be moved to the clinical team cheaply, which is the point of the distinction.

optionFeedback.b: Jensen and Meckling never assume zero agency costs; decentralization is justified when the information gain outweighs them, not because they vanish.
optionFeedback.c: Centralization is sometimes the better choice—when knowledge is general, consistency matters or interests diverge. “Always” misreads a trade-off as a rule.
optionFeedback.d: Bed counts are general knowledge that can be sent cheaply to the clinical team; the framework uses them, it does not exclude them.

check.prompt: A company documents its quarterly pricing decision using RAPID and lists five executives in the Agree role. What is the most likely consequence?

Faster decisions, because more people have approved in advance
No effect, because Agree roles are informational only
The Decide role becomes unnecessary, because the Agree holders jointly decide

check.explanation: In RAPID, Agree is a formal veto. Five vetoes multiply the ways a decision can stall and blur ownership, recreating the gridlock the tool was meant to prevent. The practitioner advice is to reserve Agree for genuine non-negotiable constraints, such as legal or safety sign-off.

optionFeedback.b: Each Agree holder can block or delay; adding vetoes slows decisions rather than speeding them.
optionFeedback.c: Agree is not informational—that is the Informed role. Agree carries the power to block.
optionFeedback.d: RAPID keeps a single Decide role precisely to avoid collective ownership; multiple vetoes undermine it rather than replace it.

lessons.title: Does Management Matter? Practices, Measures and Their Limits
lessons.summary: Structured management practices—monitoring, targets and people management—predict productivity and, in a randomized experiment, raised it; but measures that become targets invite gaming, and practices decay unless people and routines sustain them.
objectives: Describe how the World Management Survey measures management practices and what its correlations do and do not show.
Interpret the randomized management experiment in Indian textile firms and its long-run follow-up, including the limits on generalizing from them.
Diagnose metric gaming with Goodhart’s law and the multitask incentive problem, and design an operating rhythm with countermeasures.
lessons.executive: Management practices are not soft. Double-blind interviews across hundreds of firms show that structured monitoring, clear targets and merit-based people management go with higher productivity and survival, and a randomized experiment in Indian textile plants found that introducing such practices raised productivity within a year. The same research carries two warnings. A follow-up years later found that about half the adopted practices had been dropped, often after managers left. And measures turned into targets invite gaming, especially when some important work is hard to measure. Your task is to build a rhythm of review that uses measures, audits them and protects the work they miss.

explore.text: Within the same narrow industry, in the same country, some firms produce far more from the same inputs than others. Economists long treated much of that gap as a residual labelled “productivity.” Nicholas Bloom and John Van Reenen asked whether ordinary management practices could explain part of it, and built a way to measure them. In their first large survey, of 732 medium-sized manufacturing firms in the United States, France, Germany and the United Kingdom, management quality varied widely within every country, with a long tail of very badly managed firms. Better scores went with higher productivity, profitability, market valuation and survival. Poor practices were more common where competition was weak and where family firms handed control to the eldest son.

If basic practices—tracking performance, setting sensible targets, promoting and rewarding on merit—are so strongly associated with performance, a puzzle follows. Why do so many firms not adopt them? Either the practices do not really cause the performance, or something stops firms from adopting them.
Before reading on: list three reasons a profitable, family-run manufacturer might not adopt practices that would raise its productivity. Then rank them by how easy each would be to fix.

understand.text: Measuring management

The method matters because management is easy to talk about and hard to measure. Interviewers held conversational, open-ended telephone interviews with plant managers and scored 18 practices on a defined 1-to-5 grid covering monitoring, targets and people management. The design was double-blind in two senses: managers were not told they were being scored, and interviewers did not know the firm’s performance in advance. The aim was to limit both flattering answers and scores colored by what the interviewer already believed.

understand.caption: Three families of management practice (APERTURE’s paraphrase)
headers: What a low score looks like
What a high score looks like
rows: Performance is tracked informally and reviewed rarely; problems are fixed after they recur
Performance is tracked continuously and reviewed on a regular cadence; problems trigger a structured fix
Goals are vague, short-term or set without regard to what the unit controls
Goals are clear, balanced across financial and non-financial outcomes, stretching but achievable, and linked across levels
Pay and promotion follow tenure; poor performers stay; talent is not deliberately attracted
Rewards and promotion follow performance; poor performance is addressed; talent is developed and retained
understand.note: Paraphrase for teaching; this is not the survey’s scoring grid.

understand.text: From correlation to cause

Correlation leaves the obvious objection open: perhaps successful firms can afford good management, or good managers choose good firms. Bloom and colleagues addressed it with a field experiment in large Indian textile firms. Plants chosen at random received several months of free, intensive consulting to adopt a defined set of operational management practices; control plants received only the initial diagnostic. The published article reports that adopting the practices raised productivity by 17 percent in the first year, through better quality, higher efficiency and lower inventory, and that within three years treated firms opened more production plants. The authors concluded that the main barrier had been informational: owners did not know the practices or doubted they would pay. Earlier working-paper versions reported a smaller first-year figure—a reminder to cite the version you actually read.

understand.caption: The evidence ladder on management practices

steps.label: Measure
steps.text: Double-blind interviews score practices; scores vary widely and predict performance (2007).

steps.label: Test
steps.text: Randomly chosen plants get help adopting practices; productivity rises in the first year (2013).

steps.label: Revisit
steps.text: About nine years later, roughly half the practices have been dropped, yet treated plants still lead (2020).

steps.label: Generalize?
steps.text: Open question: how far results from large textile plants travel to services and knowledge work.

understand.text: A follow-up returned to the same firms about nine years after the experiment. Roughly half of the practices adopted in the experimental plants had been dropped, yet a large and significant gap with the control plants remained. Practices had spread within firms, from the experimental plants to the firms’ other plants, but few had spread across firms. Among the reasons most often given for dropping practices were turnover among managers and a lack of the directors’ time. Practices, in other words, live in people.
When measures become targets

Every management system runs on measures, and every measure invites a response. [Week 2](#w02-l3) treated this as a problem of individual incentives; here it becomes a property of the whole management system. [Goodhart’s law](#gl:g-goodharts-law), named for the economist Charles Goodhart, is usually quoted in a paraphrase: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. It is an observation, not a theorem. Its mechanism is simple: once rewards or reputations depend on a number, people look for the cheapest ways to move the number, and the cheapest ways are often not the ones that improve the outcome the number was meant to track.

Bengt Holmström and Paul Milgrom gave the observation a precise economic form, the [multitask problem](#gl:g-multitask-problem). When an employee divides effort across several tasks and only some are measurable, strong incentives on the measurable tasks pull effort away from the unmeasured ones. Their model implies that the best incentive may be weaker than intuition suggests—sometimes a fixed salary—when important tasks are hard to measure, and that jobs should group tasks of similar measurability. Incentive strength, the measurability of tasks and the assignment of tasks to jobs have to be chosen together.

understand.caption: Measurability against importance: where gaming risk concentrates
y: Task matters little to the real goal
Task matters a lot to the real goal
cells: Low stakes: measure lightly or not at all
Ignore unless it signals something larger
Measure and reward—but audit for gaming
Highest risk: incentives elsewhere will starve this task; protect it with judgment-based review, weaker incentives or a dedicated role
understand.note: APERTURE teaching device based on the multitask logic.

items: Hypothetical: a call center rewarded on average handle time sees agents end difficult calls early; customers call back and total workload rises.
Hypothetical: a hospital penalized on readmissions sees more returning patients kept in observation status; the measure improves while care may not.
Hypothetical: a software team judged on story points finds estimates inflating; reported velocity rises while delivery does not.
Hypothetical: a law firm that promotes on billable hours sees associates bill more and train juniors less.
Hypothetical: a police unit judged on clearance rates gravitates to easy cases.

understand.text: Operating rhythm

Practices become real through an [operating rhythm](#gl:g-operating-rhythm): the recurring cadence of meetings, reviews and decisions through which an organization looks at its measures, decides what to do and follows up. A common practitioner design—not a research finding—layers the rhythm by time horizon, so that each meeting answers one kind of question with the data suited to it and exercises a defined set of decision rights.

understand.caption: A layered operating rhythm (practitioner design)
rows: What is blocked today, and who unblocks it?
Are we on track, and what needs escalation?
Are outcomes moving, and are the measures still honest?
Lagging outcomes, audit samples, qualitative review
Are we doing the right work at all?
Outcome trends, external change, results of experiments
Executive team changes priorities or structure
understand.note: Practitioner design for teaching; cadences should match the work’s own clock.

blocks.text: In an observational comparison, firms that adopt a practice differ from firms that do not in many ways—owner talent, finances, markets—any of which could explain their performance. Randomly assigning the practice, or help in adopting it, makes the two groups alike on average in everything except the assignment, so a difference in outcomes can be attributed to it. Randomization does not guarantee that the result will hold elsewhere; it guarantees only that, within the study, the comparison is fair. [Week 4](#w04-l3) covered the logic in detail.

understand.title: Methodological note: reading the management experiment carefully

blocks.text: Three features limit what the textile experiment can show. The sample was small—28 plants across 17 firms—so the estimate is uncertain even though randomization makes it unbiased. The firms were large plants in one industry and one country, starting from low levels of structured management, which is exactly where gains from basic practices should be largest. And the treatment bundled many practices with months of expert attention, so the experiment cannot say which practice mattered, or how much of the effect came from the consultants’ presence rather than the practices themselves.

None of this undermines the core finding; it defines its scope. The survey evidence shows that the association is broad; the experiment shows that, in at least one setting, the arrow runs from practices to productivity; the follow-up shows that the effect can last while the practices partly decay. What these three studies cannot tell you is the size of the effect in a professional services firm, a hospital department or a sports organization. That is a question for your own careful comparisons.

understand.title: Executive twist: the dashboard that started winning

blocks.text: Six months after you introduce a monthly performance review, the department’s headline measure has improved every month. Then a frontline supervisor tells you, privately, that people now route difficult cases to another unit so they do not count. You have no audit data, and the improvement has already been reported upward. You cannot yet know how widespread the routing is. A defensible response does three things at once: it samples cases directly to estimate the size of the problem, it adds a paired measure that would reveal the routing (transfers out, for example), and it tells your own manager now that the headline number may be overstated—before someone else does.

challenge.text: The management research reopens a debate with [Lesson 1](#w08-l1). Bloom and Van Reenen’s scoring grid treats some practices as better almost everywhere—a view sometimes summarized as management as a technology. Contingency theory holds that the right practice depends on the task and environment. Both positions have support: structured practices are associated with performance across many firms and countries, yet the grid was built around work, such as manufacturing, where standardization pays well. In knowledge work with high uncertainty, a practice such as tight monitoring of individual output may be less valuable, or harmful, if it pushes effort toward what is measurable. Treat the practices as strong defaults whose fit you check, not as universal laws.

Second, many organizations already know what good practice looks like; their constraint is not information but attention and incentives. The follow-up evidence is a reminder that practices depend on the people who sustain them. Third, every measurement system has a cost: time spent reporting is time not spent working, and dashboards create the illusion that what is measured is what matters. The goal is not more measurement but measurement that people still trust after it has been tied to their rewards.

A systems view sharpens the point. A measure tied to rewards sits inside a feedback loop: the number shapes behavior, behavior shapes the number, and the organization reads the number to decide what to reward next. When gaming moves the number, the loop reinforces itself—leaders see improvement, strengthen the incentive and invite more gaming—while the outcome the number once tracked drifts out of view. A balancing loop has to be designed in deliberately: an audit, a paired measure or a qualitative review that feeds the underlying reality back into the decision. Most metric failures are loop failures, not arithmetic failures.

Finally, notice what Goodhart’s law does *not* imply. It does not mean measures are useless or that judgment should replace data; unmeasured organizations are not ungamed, they are gamed invisibly. It means a measure used for decisions needs protection: pairing with a counter-measure, periodic audit of the underlying reality, qualitative review, and a willingness to retire a measure once it has been gamed.

apply.text: Suppose you lead a hypothetical hospital’s clinical analytics department of twelve people and want structured management without gaming. A workable design: a ten-minute daily huddle on blocked requests; a weekly review of leading indicators such as request turnaround and data-quality exceptions; a monthly review of outcomes—whether clinical units actually changed practice after a report—paired with a random audit of five completed analyses for correctness; and a quarterly review of the whole portfolio of work. Turnaround time is measured but not rewarded on its own, because it is easy to game by splitting requests; it is always read alongside the quality audit.

The same pattern appears in very different settings. A hypothetical public school district that rewards principals on test pass rates should expect attention to drift toward students near the pass mark; pairing the rate with growth across all students and a sample of classroom observations protects the rest. A hypothetical sales organization that pays only on bookings should expect discounting and poorly qualified deals; pairing bookings with retention a year later changes what a good quarter looks like.

A player development department faces the same structure. Measures of player progress—velocity, swing decisions, strength gains—are measurable and important, so they belong in the review. But some of the most important work is hard to measure: the quality of a coach’s relationship with a player, the long-term health effects of a training load, the transfer of skills to competition. If coaches are rewarded strongly on the measurable gains, the multitask logic predicts that effort will shift away from what cannot be measured. Countermeasures follow from the theory: pair each performance measure with a health and workload measure, review a sample of individual plans qualitatively each month, keep incentive pay modest relative to base pay, and assign the hard-to-measure work to someone whose evaluation depends on it.

retain.text: Structured monitoring, targets and people management are strongly associated with productivity, and in one randomized experiment they caused it. The effect can persist while practices decay, especially when the managers who carried them leave. Measures drive behavior: turn a measure into a target and expect gaming, most of all when important work is hard to measure. Build an operating rhythm that uses measures, audits them and protects the unmeasured work.

A randomized experiment in Indian textile plants found that adopting such practices raised productivity in the first year; the main barrier had been information.

A good operating rhythm pairs measures, audits them and assigns someone to protect the unmeasured work.

options.text: It shows that the practices raise productivity in every industry

It proves that practices last indefinitely once adopted
It shows that informational barriers are the only reason firms fail to adopt practices

optionFeedback.a: Randomization secures internal validity, not external validity; one industry in one country cannot show effects everywhere.
optionFeedback.c: The nine-year follow-up found that roughly half the adopted practices had been dropped.
optionFeedback.d: The authors identify information as the main barrier, not the only one; they also point to limited managerial time.

check.prompt: A clinic pays physicians a large bonus based on patient visits per day. Care coordination—calls to specialists, reviewing test results, family meetings—is important but not counted. What does the multitask model predict?

options.text: Visits rise and coordination falls
Both rise, because motivated physicians work harder overall
Nothing changes, because professionals ignore incentives
Coordination rises, because physicians want to justify the bonus

The model’s remedies are weaker incentives on visits, measures that capture coordination, or assigning coordination to a role evaluated on it.

optionFeedback.b: Total effort may rise somewhat, but the model’s central prediction is reallocation toward the rewarded task at the expense of the unrewarded one.
optionFeedback.c: Professionals respond to incentives too; the multitask model applies to any agent dividing effort across tasks.
optionFeedback.d: Nothing in the bonus rewards coordination, so the model predicts the opposite.

lessons.title: Routines, Culture and Teams: The Organization Beneath the Chart
lessons.summary: Organizations remember through routines, which make them reliable and also resistant to change; teams perform best when leaders design the conditions—a real team, direction, structure, context and coaching—rather than rely on personal style.
objectives: Explain how routines store organizational knowledge and why reorganizations and turnover can erase it.
Diagnose a team against Hackman’s five conditions and propose design changes.
Distinguish structural team design from team climate, connecting design choices to the psychological safety material from Week 5.
lessons.executive: Below every organization chart lies the organization that actually runs: routines—repeated patterns of interdependent action—that store what the organization knows and settle who does what without constant renegotiation. Routines make organizations reliable, and they make them slow to change. That is why reorganizations and the departure of key people can destroy capability that appears in no document. Teams are where many routines are built. Hackman’s work suggests that a leader’s main lever is not personal style but conditions: a real team with stable membership, a compelling direction, an enabling structure, a supportive context and expert coaching. Design the conditions, then protect the routines that work.

explore.text: Two hypothetical intensive care units in the same hospital system follow the same written protocols, have similar staffing ratios and report to the same chief nursing officer. One reliably catches deteriorating patients early; the other does not. A visitor who spends a week in both notices the difference in small things. In the first unit, the night charge nurse walks every room at three in the morning and asks each nurse one question; the respiratory therapist joins rounds without being invited; new nurses are paired with the same mentor for six weeks. None of this is in the protocol. All of it is how the unit actually works.

The previous lesson ended with a puzzle from the textile follow-up: practices that demonstrably paid off were dropped when the managers who carried them left. This lesson explains why. Formal design—structure, decision rights, measures—creates the frame. What fills the frame is a set of routines that people build and maintain, often without noticing that they are doing so.
Before reading on: think of the best-run team you have worked in. Write down three things it did repeatedly that no policy required. Would those habits survive if its leader left?

understand.text: Routines as organizational memory

Richard Nelson and Sidney Winter placed routines at the center of their evolutionary theory of the firm. Routines are the regular, predictable patterns of activity through which an organization does its work, from how it schedules production to how it decides what to investigate next. They argued that routines are the main way organizations store operational knowledge—much of it tacit, held in coordinated habits rather than documents—which makes routines the organizational counterpart of an individual’s skills. Routines are also a truce: they settle, for the time being, conflicts over who does what, so that work can proceed without constant renegotiation.

Two implications follow. Routines make organizations reliable, because coordinated action does not need to be re-planned every time. And routines make organizations resistant to change, because changing a routine reopens the truce and discards knowledge no one wrote down. In Nelson and Winter’s account, firms grow or shrink as competition selects among their routines, which is why capabilities are hard to copy and why organizations often change more slowly than their environments.

understand.caption: How a practice becomes part of the organization

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: A leader introduces a practice—for example, a weekly case review.

steps.label: Repetition
steps.text: People perform it on a cadence; mistakes are corrected.

steps.label: Routine
steps.text: It runs without the leader; roles and hand-offs are tacitly understood.

steps.label: Norm
steps.text: Skipping it feels wrong; newcomers learn it by watching.

steps.label: Risk
steps.text: If the routine stops fitting the work, the same stability becomes inertia.

understand.caption: Routine strength against environmental change
cells: Wasted effort: every case improvised and quality varies
Improvisation without memory: adaptable, but lessons are lost
Reliable efficiency: the organization performs well and cheaply
Competence trap: well-practiced routines that no longer fit

understand.text: Culture, practically defined

Culture is one of the most used and least precise words in management. For design purposes, APERTURE uses a working definition: culture is the set of shared assumptions about what is rewarded, what is tolerated and how work really gets done, made visible in routines. The definition is deliberately behavioral. It suggests that you learn a culture by watching which routines persist when no one is checking, what happens to someone who raises bad news, and which rules are actually enforced. It also suggests that culture changes mainly when routines, rewards and decision rights change, not when a values statement does.
Designing teams

J. Richard Hackman spent decades studying work teams, and his central claim runs against much popular leadership advice: how well a team performs depends less on the leader’s personal style than on whether the leader has designed and supported the team so its members can manage themselves. He summarized the conditions in five parts, which he presented as guiding principles to apply to each situation rather than a formula.

understand.caption: Hackman’s five conditions, with diagnostic questions
rows: Clear boundaries, genuine interdependence, reasonably stable membership
Can every member name every other member, and does the work make them depend on one another?
A clear, challenging and consequential purpose
Could members state what the team exists to achieve, in one sentence, consistently?
A well-designed task, the right size and mix of members, and clear norms of conduct
Is the team the right size with the right skills, and are a few core norms explicit?
Rewards, information, training and resources from the wider organization
Does the organization reward team results, and can the team get the data and resources it needs?
Competent help with how the team works together, when the team can use it
Does anyone help the team review how it works, not only what it produces?
understand.note: Conditions as summarized from Hackman (2002); the diagnostic questions are APERTURE’s.

understand.text: Hackman’s conditions are structural, and they interact with team climate. [Week 5](#w05-l2) examined psychological safety—a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking—and the evidence on how it relates to learning. The design lesson is that structure and climate need each other. Structure creates the channels through which bad news and new ideas can travel: a review routine, a defined role for raising risks, a decision owner who must respond. Climate determines whether anyone uses the channels. A team with a perfect charter and a leader who punishes dissent will not learn; a team with a warm climate and no routine for reviewing its errors will feel good and repeat them.

blocks.text: Not every group is a team. A *working group* is a set of people who share information but are individually accountable for separate outputs—a committee of department heads, for example. A *team* shares a collective output and depends on its members’ interdependent work. A *crew* is a team whose members are interchangeable experts who can perform together immediately because roles are highly standardized, like a flight crew or a surgical team assembled for one shift. Calling a working group a team, or expecting a crew to behave like a long-standing team, is a common design error. These definitions are APERTURE’s teaching distinctions.

understand.title: Methodological note: why evidence on routines and teams is hard to pin down

blocks.text: Routines are difficult to measure because they are partly tacit; much of the research on them is qualitative, historical or theoretical, which makes it strong on mechanism and weak on effect sizes. Team research faces its own problems. Many studies rely on members’ surveys about both team processes and team performance, which inflates associations because the same people report both. Teams are not randomly assigned to good or bad conditions; well-run organizations tend to create better conditions and better results at the same time. Hackman’s conditions are best read as a well-grounded framework for diagnosis, drawn from extensive field research, rather than as a set of separately estimated causal effects.

challenge.text: The routine-centered view has critics. If routines explain everything that persists, the concept risks becoming a label for whatever we observe. And routines are not only stabilizing: the people who perform them adjust them constantly, so the line between a routine and an improvisation is blurrier than the theory suggests. For a leader, the practical tension is real: the routines that make a unit reliable are the same ones that make it resist a needed change.

Culture claims deserve particular skepticism. Statements such as “culture eats strategy” are slogans, not findings. When a culture explanation is offered for a failure, ask what specific routine, reward or decision right produced the behavior. If the explanation cannot name one, it may be a way of avoiding a harder diagnosis—or of blaming the people who work inside a system for the system’s design.

Teams have limits as well. Teams incur coordination costs and process losses; for work that is truly individual, a team design adds meetings without adding value. Stable membership, one of Hackman’s conditions, collides with organizations that move people often across projects. And the five conditions say little about the politics of who gets onto a team or who is left off, which can shape performance as much as the charter does.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the routine only one person knows

blocks.text: A high-performing unit depends on one veteran coordinator who runs the weekly case review, maintains the master schedule and knows which exceptions matter. She announces she will retire in four months. No one has documented what she does, and asking her to write it all down will capture the rules but not the judgment. Your budget is limited and you cannot hire a replacement before she leaves. You could pair a successor with her for every review, record the routine as it runs, split her role across two people, or redesign the routine so it depends less on one person. Each option protects a different kind of knowledge; the mistake is to treat her departure as a staffing problem rather than a design problem.

apply.text: Use Hackman’s conditions to diagnose a hypothetical hospital rapid-response team that is called to deteriorating patients on general wards. It is a real team only on paper: membership rotates daily, so the same nurse, respiratory therapist and physician rarely work together twice. Its direction is clear—rescue patients before cardiac arrest—but its structure is weak: no agreed roles at the bedside, no norm about who speaks first. The context undermines it: ward managers are judged on how rarely their wards call the team. And no one reviews its cases. A design response changes the conditions, not the people: fixed pairings for a month at a time, a short bedside role script, removing the measure that discourages calls, and a weekly fifteen-minute case review. None of this requires a more charismatic leader.

The same lens works elsewhere. A hypothetical technology company’s on-call engineering rotation can be a real team with enabling routines—blameless incident reviews, clear escalation norms—or merely a list of names attached to a pager. Military and emergency organizations that hold after-action reviews are maintaining a routine that turns experience into shared knowledge. A hypothetical professional basketball staff that replaces most of its assistants every season loses its tacit routines with each departure, whatever the playbook says.

In player development, much of what makes a department good lives in routines: how information about a player travels when he moves between levels, how a new coach learns the department’s methods, how staff from different disciplines decide together. These routines are vulnerable to exactly the shocks this lesson describes—turnover, reorganization and growth. Three design moves follow. Write down the hand-off routines that carry information between levels, and test them by watching a real hand-off. Pair new staff with experienced colleagues long enough to absorb the tacit parts. And treat any cross-disciplinary group around a player as a real team—stable membership, a clear purpose, defined roles and a regular review—rather than a meeting that happens when someone remembers to schedule it.

retain.text: Routines store what organizations know and settle who does what; they make organizations reliable and slow to change. Culture is best read through routines, rewards and decision rights rather than slogans. Team performance depends heavily on conditions leaders can design—a real team, compelling direction, enabling structure, supportive context and coaching—while psychological safety determines whether the channels that structure creates are actually used.

takeaways: Routines are organizational memory and a truce over who does what; they produce reliability and inertia at the same time.
Reorganizations and turnover destroy tacit routines that appear in no document—plan for the transition cost.
Culture is visible in routines, rewards and decision rights; be suspicious of culture explanations that name none of these.
Leaders shape team performance mostly through conditions: a real team, compelling direction, enabling structure, supportive context and coaching.

check.prompt: Why does Nelson and Winter’s account predict that a reorganization can reduce performance in the short term, even when the new structure is better designed?

options.text: Because it disrupts routines that store tacit knowledge and settle conflicts, and these must be rebuilt
Because employees resist every change regardless of its design
Because new structures are usually worse than the ones they replace
Because routines are written procedures that take time to rewrite

check.explanation: Routines are where much of an organization’s operational knowledge lives, largely in tacit, coordinated habits, and they also function as a truce over who does what. A reorganization breaks hand-offs and reopens that truce, so performance can dip while new routines form—even if the new design is better in the long run.

optionFeedback.b: Resistance can matter, but the routine argument holds even with willing employees: the knowledge is embedded in coordinated habits that must be rebuilt.
optionFeedback.c: The argument does not assume the new design is worse; it explains a transition cost that applies to good designs too.
optionFeedback.d: Routines are largely tacit; if they were only written procedures, they could be rewritten quickly and little knowledge would be lost.

check.prompt: A product team has a charismatic leader but rotating membership, unclear goals and no access to customer data. Following Hackman, what is the most effective first move?

options.text: Send the leader to a course on inspirational communication
Stabilize membership, clarify the team’s purpose and secure the data it needs
Replace the leader with a more directive manager
Add more members so the team has more capacity

check.explanation: Hackman’s central claim is that conditions matter more than the leader’s style. This team fails three conditions—it is not a real team, it lacks a compelling direction, and its context does not supply the information it needs. Fixing those conditions is the highest-leverage move; changing the leader’s style addresses none of them.

optionFeedback.a: This targets leader style, which Hackman argues matters less than the conditions the team is missing.
optionFeedback.c: A more directive leader does not create stable membership, a clear purpose or access to data.
optionFeedback.d: Adding members to a team without stable membership or clear goals usually increases coordination costs.
