glossary.definition: The degree to which an organization’s subunits develop different goals, time horizons, interpersonal styles and formality as each adapts to its own part of the environment.
The quality of collaboration among differentiated subunits that an organization needs to achieve unity of effort, and the mechanisms that produce it.
The view that no single structure is best; effective structure depends on fit with the organization’s task, technology and environment.
The gap between the information a task requires and the information the organization already has; in the information-processing view, it drives how much information must be processed during the work.
Deliberate spare capacity—longer lead times, buffers, less demanding targets—that reduces the need for coordination at the cost of idle resources.
Coordinating devices that let units decide together without escalating: direct contact, liaison roles, task forces, teams, integrating roles and matrix structures.

A unit given every skill and resource a product, customer or region needs, so that fewer decisions require coordination with other units; it trades duplicated specialists for a lighter information load.
A position whose job is to coordinate differentiated units—such as a bed-management coordinator or a technical director—often with authority to resolve conflicts between them without escalation.
One of Mintzberg’s five ways of aligning work: direct supervision, standardization of work processes, outputs or skills, and mutual adjustment.
The number of people who report directly to one manager; wider spans mean fewer managers and layers but less supervision and coaching per person.
The formal authority to initiate, approve, carry out or veto a decision, and the allocation of that authority across roles.
Knowledge that is costly to transmit—tacit, local or perishable—so that decisions using it are best made by the people who hold it; contrasted with cheaply transmitted general knowledge.
The cost that arises when a principal delegates to an agent with different interests: monitoring and incentive spending, the agent’s reassurance costs, and value lost to remaining divergence.
A practitioner heuristic that assigns, for each task or decision, who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed. Not an empirically validated instrument.
A practitioner heuristic from management consulting that assigns decision roles: Recommend, Agree (a formal veto), Perform, Input and Decide. Not an empirically validated instrument.
The observation that organizations design systems mirroring their own communication structures; studied as the mirroring hypothesis and found common but not universal.
The research program, begun by Bloom and Van Reenen, that scores firms’ monitoring, targets and people-management practices from double-blind interviews.
A regular, predictable pattern of interdependent action through which an organization does its work; it stores tacit knowledge and settles who does what.
In Hackman’s terms, a group with clear boundaries, genuinely interdependent work and reasonably stable membership—the first condition for team effectiveness.

exercise.title: Organization Builder

intro.text: You will design the Risk Intelligence department of Corlund Pay, a fictional consumer-payments and small-loan company. The department brings together fraud analytics, credit-risk modeling, independent model validation and risk reporting, which today sit in three different places. Your fully loaded staff budget is $1.5 million a year—enough for a capable department, not for a comfortable one. Every number in the exercise is synthetic.

items: Read the brief and the list of roles, work items and decisions.
Add positions under the Head of Risk Intelligence and choose who reports to whom.
Assign every work item to one or more positions. Watch hours against capacity and skills against requirements.
Assign decision roles—Recommend, Input, Decide, Informed—for each decision. Aim for exactly one Decide per decision.
Read the checks and the scenario rules, then revise. Build at least two different designs before you settle on one, and note what each one gives up.

intro.text: What to notice: which constraint binds first (budget, span, skills or hours); whether the work that runs on a minute-by-minute clock (fraud) needs a different structure from the work that runs on a quarterly clock (credit); where a single person has become a point of failure; and whether the people who build models are the same people who validate them. Connect each choice to the week’s frameworks: Galbraith’s strategies, Mintzberg’s mechanisms, span arithmetic and Jensen and Meckling’s logic of decision rights.

brief.text: Corlund Pay (fictional) offers instant payments and small consumer loans to about two million customers. Fraud analytics, credit modeling and risk reporting grew up in three different departments, and a recent fictional regulatory examination criticized the company for letting the people who build credit models also validate them. The chief risk officer has asked you to design a single Risk Intelligence department.

The work runs on two clocks. Fraud runs in minutes: attacks begin at night and on weekends, and a rule may need to change within the hour. Credit runs in quarters: model changes are tested, documented, independently validated and reported to the board’s risk committee. Both depend on the same data pipelines. The work items below total 232 hours a week. Your fully loaded staff budget is $1,500,000 a year.

Start with the Head. Add positions, assign work and assign decision roles, then read the checks. A design that passes every check can still be a poor design; a design that fails one check may be the right trade-off if you can say why.

work.label: Real-time fraud monitoring and on-call response (nights and weekends included)
Independent validation of models before release
Risk reviews for new product launches
People leadership: hiring, coaching, performance reviews
Strategy and coordination with Product, Finance and Compliance
Ad hoc analysis requests from Operations and Finance

decisions.label: Deploy a new or retrained fraud model to production
Change the credit approval cutoff for a loan product
Add an emergency fraud rule during an active attack (minutes, not days)
Approve the quarterly risk report to the board’s risk committee
Sign off the risk review for a new product launch
Reprioritize the analytics backlog between Fraud and Credit

rules.text: Independent validation: no position assigned to independent validation (w4) may also be assigned fraud or credit model development (w2, w3), or report—directly or through a chain—to a position that is. The fictional regulator treats self-validation as a finding.
Around-the-clock coverage: real-time fraud monitoring (w1) should be shared by at least two positions with fraud skills. One person cannot cover nights, weekends, illness and vacation.

Room to integrate: if more than half of the Head’s hours go to work items other than people leadership (w10) and cross-functional coordination (w11), no one is integrating Risk Intelligence with Product, Finance and Compliance.
Incentive conflict: the Product Risk Partner sits with a product team measured on loan volume. That position should not hold the Decide role on the credit cutoff (d2) or on launch sign-off (d5).
Speed: the emergency fraud rule (d3) loses value by the minute. If its Decide holder does not also carry fraud monitoring (w1) or manage the people who do, expect delay at 2 a.m.
Overload: ad hoc requests (w12) expand to fill unprotected capacity. If they are assigned to the same people who carry critical work, expect the critical work to slip in busy weeks.

debrief.text: The exercise is built so that no design satisfies every goal. The budget buys eight or nine positions, the work needs about six full-time equivalents, and the gap disappears quickly once you add a manager, an in-house validator or the coverage that around-the-clock fraud work requires. Three reference designs show the shape of the trade-offs. Each is one defensible answer, not the answer.

debrief.caption: Three reference designs (synthetic costs)
rows: A. Flat: the Head with seven specialists
Head; Senior Data Scientist; Data Scientist; Analytics Engineer; Model Validation Lead; two Fraud Operations Analysts; Risk Reporting Analyst
Span of 7, at the limit; the Head’s week is consumed by leadership, launch reviews and coordination; one engineer is a single point of failure
Low cost and short lines, paid for with a Head who has no slack and $165,000 that cannot be spent without breaking the span limit
Head; Fraud Analytics Manager; Credit Risk Manager; Fraud Operations Analyst; Data Scientist; Analytics Engineer; Risk Reporting Analyst; external validation retainer
Both managers have a span of 1, below the minimum; no position combines modeling and fraud skills for fraud model work; validation covers 12 of 18 hours
Clear domain accountability, paid for with too little modeling capacity: at this scale a management layer consumes the budget for scarce skills
C. Hybrid: a fraud unit with its own manager, credit under the Head
Head; Fraud Analytics Manager leading two Fraud Operations Analysts and the Senior Data Scientist; Data Scientist; Analytics Engineer; Risk Reporting Analyst; external validation retainer
Spans of 5 and 3; the fraud unit can decide quickly on its own clock; validation covers 12 of 18 hours; one engineer remains a single point of failure
Differentiates the fast-clock fraud work, paid for with thinner validation; swapping the retainer for an in-house lead fits the budget only if the reporting analyst goes
debrief.note: Synthetic data. Costs are the role costs listed in the exercise; hours and spans follow the exercise’s rules.

debrief.text: Design C uses Lawrence and Lorsch’s logic: the fraud work is differentiated enough—different clock, different supervision, different decisions—to justify its own unit and a local Decide right on emergency rules, while the credit work stays close to the Head, who carries the board relationship. Design A uses Galbraith’s vertical logic: a single leader integrates everything, which works until exceptions pile up. Design B shows a classic error at small scale: copying a structure built for a larger organization. Layers are a fixed cost; they pay off only when spans are wide enough to need them.

What the exercise does not show. The checks are arithmetic and scenario rules, not predictions of how real people would perform. The Builder cannot see informal power, the trust between the fraud and credit groups, the quality of the people you hire, or the routines they would build. It treats hours as interchangeable when they are not: a night shift costs more in fatigue than a day shift. And it holds the budget fixed, when in practice a strong case could change it. Use the Builder to expose trade-offs and make them explicit, not to certify a design.

The same exercise transfers directly to a development or baseball operations department: work on different clocks (game-day and daily work versus seasonal planning), scarce specialized skills, a need for independent review of analytical work, and a budget that forces a choice between managers and specialists. The Week 14 capstone reuses this tool for a department of your own design.

assumptions: All costs are synthetic, fully loaded annual figures in US dollars (salary, benefits, equipment).
Hours are weekly hours available for assigned work; routine administration beyond the listed work items is assumed absorbed.
Work items may be split across positions; a critical item held by only one position is flagged as a single point of failure.
The independence of model validation is a rule of this fictional scenario, not a statement about the requirements of any real regulator or jurisdiction.
Checks and scenario rules are transparent arithmetic and stated assumptions, not validated predictions of organizational performance.

case.title: Fourteen Front Doors
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. Numbers are synthetic and chosen for teaching.

body.text: Renata Solís had been Merrowby Health’s chief integration officer for eleven weeks when the board chair put the question plainly. In six weeks, management would present its recommendation on how Quarryline Community Clinics would fit into Merrowby’s new structure. The board had approved the new structure in principle. It had no appetite for another year of debate about what that meant.

Merrowby is a regional system of three hospitals and about 9,000 employees. For decades it was organized by function: a chief nursing officer, a chief medical officer and a chief operating officer ran their disciplines across all three hospitals, and each hospital had a president responsible for its building and budget. Eighteen months ago Merrowby acquired Quarryline, a network of fourteen primary-care and urgent-care clinics founded by a group of physicians, which had grown by letting each clinic largely run itself. Last spring the board approved a move to *service lines*—Cardiovascular, Orthopedics and Spine, Oncology, Women’s and Children’s, and Primary and Community Care—each led by a physician paired with an administrator.
On paper, Quarryline was the obvious core of the new Primary and Community Care service line. In practice, nobody agreed on what that meant.

Each Quarryline clinic has a lead physician who sets the clinic’s schedule templates, hires its medical assistants and front-desk staff, and runs a ten-minute huddle every morning to review the day’s patients, open test results and staffing gaps. Clinic leads meet monthly as a group, chaired by Quarryline’s founder, Dr. Tomas Achterberg, who still sees patients two days a week. Physicians are paid a salary plus a bonus tied to a short list of quality measures and patient experience. Patients can usually reach “their” nurse by phone. The clinics run their own instance of the electronic health record, configured over years by the clinicians themselves.

Quarryline’s results are good and uneven (Exhibit 1). Its cost per visit is lower than that of Merrowby’s hospital-based clinics, and its patient-experience scores are higher. But the share of patients with diabetes whose blood sugar is under control varies widely from clinic to clinic, and about two in five referrals from Quarryline physicians go to specialists outside Merrowby—often, Quarryline physicians say, because Merrowby’s specialists take weeks to see new patients and rarely send notes back.

Gwen Halloran, Merrowby’s chief financial officer, favors full integration. Under her proposal, Quarryline’s clinics would move to Merrowby’s standard model within twelve months: one central scheduling call center, standard visit templates, migration to Merrowby’s electronic record, and physician pay moved to Merrowby’s productivity model, which pays mainly on work units per visit. Clinic leads would report to three new regional directors. Her team estimates annual savings of about $6.8 million once the work is complete, mostly from purchasing, the call center and retiring the second record system (Exhibit 2). “We bought a network,” she told Renata. “Right now we own fourteen small businesses.”

Dr. Achterberg argues the opposite. He wants Quarryline kept as a distinct division with its own leadership, controlling schedules, clinic staffing and physician pay, integrating only finance and purchasing now and the electronic record on a slower timeline. He has a warning: two clinic leads resigned in the past quarter, and he says more will follow if “the call center and the productivity machine” arrive. A recent engagement survey supports him, although only 41 percent of Quarryline clinicians answered it. Specialists inside Merrowby find his position frustrating. The chief of cardiology says Quarryline behaves “like a referral source we have to court, not part of the same system.”

Dr. Priya Marchetti, the chief medical officer, and Owen Bakshi, the chief operating officer, have sketched a third approach. A short list of *system decisions*—the electronic record, clinical quality measures, referral pathways, credentialing and purchasing—would be set centrally. A list of *local decisions*—daily schedules within agreed access standards, hiring of support staff, huddles, and how each clinic meets its quality targets—would stay with clinic leads. Nurse navigators would sit between the clinics and each specialty service line, responsible for getting referred patients seen quickly and making sure notes come back. Physician pay would blend salary, quality and a modest productivity component. Owen likes the design but worries about who manages whom: a single vice president for Primary and Community Care would have fourteen clinic leads, six urgent-care medical directors and the navigation team reporting directly, unless another layer is added. Gwen calls the hybrid “the expensive way to get half the savings.”

Last autumn, two Quarryline clinics volunteered to route their phones through Merrowby’s central call center for four months. The results are in Exhibit 3. Abandoned calls fell sharply and more same-day appointments were filled. Complaints about being unable to reach the care team tripled, though from a low base. One of the two pilot clinic leads was among those who resigned—for reasons, he said, that had “a lot to do with the phones and a little to do with everything else.” Gwen sees a successful pilot. Dr. Achterberg sees a warning. Renata sees two volunteer clinics, no comparison group chosen in advance and four months of data.

Renata’s list of unknowns is long. She does not know how much of the referral leakage is about access and how much about long-standing relationships that a navigator cannot replace. She does not know whether the variation in diabetes control reflects clinic practices or the patients each clinic serves; Quarryline’s two lowest-scoring clinics serve the poorest neighborhoods in the region. She does not know whether the savings estimates include the cost of physicians who leave. By Merrowby’s own internal estimate, recruiting and onboarding a primary-care physician costs about $250,000, and a new physician takes a year or more to build a full panel. Each option’s estimate was prepared by its sponsor, and none has been reviewed independently. And she does not know how the board will react to a recommendation that defers some savings.

She also knows what each option would do to the people who carry Quarryline’s routines. The morning huddles, the clinic leads’ monthly meeting and the nurses who know their patients by name appear in no integration plan. If those routines are what keep Quarryline’s costs low and its patients satisfied, a design that erases them could save money on paper and lose it in practice. If, instead, those same routines are part of why referrals leave the system and quality varies, preserving them unchanged would protect the problem along with the strengths.

On Friday, Renata blocks two hours to draft her recommendation. It must say which decisions belong to the system and which to the clinics, who reports to whom, how physicians will be paid and measured, how fast integration will move, and what evidence would make Merrowby change course.

questions: Using Lawrence and Lorsch and Galbraith, how differentiated are Quarryline’s clinics from Merrowby’s specialty service lines, and which integrating mechanisms does each option rely on?

Sort the decisions in play—schedules, support-staff hiring, physician pay, the electronic record, referral pathways, quality measures—into system and local decisions using Jensen and Meckling’s logic. Where would you depart from the hybrid proposal, and why?
What does the multitask model predict if Quarryline physicians move to productivity-based pay? What would you measure to detect the effect early?
How much weight should the call-center pilot carry? Design a better test, and say whether any part of it could be run before the board meeting.
Which Quarryline routines are most at risk under each option, and which of them are worth protecting?

perspectives.title: Integrate fast and manage the departures
perspectives.text: A system that keeps two operating models pays for both indefinitely, and the longest delays are where integrations die. Full integration captures most of the savings, ends referral leakage by routing patients through one scheduling system, and makes quality variation visible on one record. Departures are a real cost, but some turnover is the price of any merger; the response is retention agreements for the strongest clinic leads, not a protected division. The weakness of this position is that it treats Quarryline’s routines as overhead and its pay model as a detail, and the multitask logic predicts that productivity pay will crowd out the coordination work that keeps patients well.

perspectives.title: Protect what works and earn integration
perspectives.text: Quarryline’s low cost and high patient experience are evidence that its decentralized model works, and its routines—huddles, a nurse patients can reach, physician control of schedules—are the mechanism. Integrating finance and purchasing captures the easy savings without touching them. Referral leakage is better solved by fixing specialist access, which is Merrowby’s problem, than by controlling Quarryline’s schedules. The weakness is that a protected division can harden into a permanent separate company, leaving diabetes-control variation and referral leakage unaddressed and the system paying for two of everything.

perspectives.title: Split the decisions, then sequence
perspectives.text: The hybrid applies Jensen and Meckling directly: centralize decisions where knowledge is general and consistency matters (the record, quality measures, credentialing, referral pathways), and leave decisions where knowledge is specific and local (daily schedules, huddles, support staff) with the clinics. Navigators are a lateral integrating role aimed at the leakage problem. The span problem is solvable with two regional leads drawn from Quarryline’s own clinic leads. The weakness is cost, and the risk that a long list of system decisions grows each year until the hybrid becomes full integration by stealth.

perspectives.title: Test before committing
perspectives.text: The evidence on the table cannot settle the question: a four-month pilot with two volunteer clinics, a survey with a low response rate and savings estimates prepared by sponsors. Commit now only to the decisions every option shares—purchasing, finance, credentialing—and roll out navigators and central scheduling in a staggered sequence across clinics, with the order chosen at random and outcomes compared, before deciding the rest. The weakness is time: the board wants a decision, staggered rollouts take a year, and uncertainty itself may drive clinicians away.

case.application: The same structure appears when a baseball organization integrates a unit that grew up on its own terms—a newly affiliated club, an international academy, or a department formed by merging two groups with different working rhythms. The useful questions are the case’s questions: which decisions must be consistent across the organization and which depend on local, specific knowledge; which integrating mechanism (a coordinator role, a shared information system, a common player plan) addresses the actual coordination failure; how a change in how staff are measured and paid will shift effort between measurable and unmeasurable work; and which local routines carry knowledge that no integration plan has written down. The case also models a discipline worth keeping: a small, self-selected pilot is a reason to design a better test, not proof.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Lawrence and Lorsch’s conclusion about differentiation and integration in effective organizations?

options.text: Effective organizations minimize differentiation so that integration becomes unnecessary
Effective organizations achieve the differentiation their environment demands and invest in integration to match it
Integration matters only in stable environments; in turbulent ones, units should operate independently
Differentiation and integration are two names for the same property of structure

questions.explanation: Lawrence and Lorsch found that effective organizations did not avoid differentiation; they achieved the degree their environment required and then achieved the integration needed to hold differentiated units together. Because differentiated units see the world differently, the more differentiation a firm needs, the more deliberate its integration must be.

optionFeedback.a: Minimizing differentiation would sacrifice the specialized adaptation each unit needs; the effective organizations were not the least differentiated.
optionFeedback.c: Turbulent, diverse environments tend to require more differentiation, which makes integration harder and more important, not irrelevant.
optionFeedback.d: They pull in opposite directions: differentiation is the divergence of units, integration the collaboration that reconnects them.

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis best fits this situation?

stimulus.text: A city government merges its building-permit office, which processes thousands of standard applications under fixed rules, with its urban-innovation unit, which runs small, ambiguous pilot projects with outside partners. After the merger, the permit office’s procedures are applied to the innovation unit: every pilot needs a standard application, three sign-offs and a 30-day review. Within a year, two partners abandon pilots and the innovation unit’s strongest staff transfer out. The permit office’s performance is unchanged. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: The merger imposed coordination by standardized work processes on work that depends on mutual adjustment
The innovation unit was not differentiated enough from the permit office
The merged unit’s span of control was too wide
The innovation unit needed stronger output targets to stay accountable

questions.explanation: The permit office is close to a machine bureaucracy: standardized processes suit routine, high-volume work. The innovation unit is closer to an adhocracy, which coordinates through mutual adjustment because its work is uncertain. Applying one mechanism to both erased a legitimate differentiation and overloaded uncertain work with procedures—an integration failure dressed as standardization.

optionFeedback.b: The problem is the reverse: the units were appropriately differentiated, and the merger forced them into the same mode of coordination.
optionFeedback.c: Nothing in the scenario points to span; the failure comes from the coordinating mechanism applied to the work.
optionFeedback.d: Output targets are another form of standardization; the unit’s problem was too much standardization for uncertain work, not too little accountability.

questions.prompt: An operations division has 600 frontline employees. Leadership is comparing an average span of control of 6 with an average span of 10. Rounding up at each level until a single executive remains, how many fewer managers (including the executive) does the span-10 design need?
questions.explanation: The span-10 design needs 67 managers in three layers; the span-6 design needs 121 in four layers, so widening the span removes 54 positions and one layer. The saving is real, but each remaining manager must now absorb more exceptions and coaching. Whether that works depends on how standardized the work is and whether information systems and lateral links take up the load.

questions.prompt: In Jensen and Meckling’s framework, an organization should move a decision right closer to frontline employees when…

options.text: the knowledge needed is general and easy to send to headquarters
the fall in costs from poorly informed decisions exceeds the rise in agency costs from delegating
frontline employees ask for more autonomy
the decision strongly affects many other units

questions.explanation: Jensen and Meckling frame the location of decision rights as a trade-off: moving rights toward specific knowledge lowers the cost of poor information but raises agency costs. Delegation is justified when the first gain exceeds the second, and it should come with measurement and rewards that contain the agency costs.

optionFeedback.a: When knowledge is general it can be moved cheaply to the center, which weakens the case for delegating.
optionFeedback.c: A request for autonomy may matter for motivation, but it is not the criterion in this framework.
optionFeedback.d: High interdependence usually favors central coordination, because local decisions impose costs on other units.

questions.prompt: What is the best next move?

stimulus.text: You lead analytics at a hypothetical mid-sized insurer. Your team has built a fraud-risk score that feeds a single shared investigation queue staffed by one team, so only one threshold can be set. Underwriting wants a low threshold, flagging more cases; Claims wants a high one, so investigators see fewer cases. Both vice presidents report to the chief operating officer. The score launches in three weeks, and no one has defined who decides the threshold.

options.text: Set the threshold yourself, since your team built the model and understands it best

Propose a written allocation for this decision to the chief operating officer: your team Recommends with evidence on the trade-offs, both vice presidents give Input, one named executive Decides, and a review date is set
Ask Underwriting and Claims to negotiate until they reach consensus, delaying launch if necessary
Launch with the midpoint between the two preferred thresholds and revisit if anyone complains

questions.explanation: The failure is a missing decision owner for a choice that crosses units with conflicting interests. Making the allocation explicit—who recommends, whose input is required, who decides, when it will be reviewed—solves that without redesigning the organization. Your team holds the technical knowledge, so it should recommend and lay out the trade-off; the decision itself is about the organization’s appetite for risk and cost, which belongs to someone accountable for both units.

optionFeedback.a: Your team holds the technical knowledge but not the authority over the business trade-off between two units; deciding it yourself invites a challenge after launch.
optionFeedback.c: Consensus between units with opposed interests and no owner is the slowest path, and it may never arrive.
optionFeedback.d: Splitting the difference hides the trade-off and leaves no one accountable; it is a decision made by default.

questions.prompt: What is the main flaw in the consultant’s argument?

stimulus.text: A consultant tells a hospital system (hypothetical): “Conway’s law proves that a system’s design always mirrors the organization that built it. Our electronic record is fragmented because our departments are fragmented. So if we reorganize into service lines, the record will integrate itself within a year, and we will not need to invest in shared data standards.”

options.text: It treats an observation that holds often but not always as a deterministic law, and ignores that shared standards and tools are a separate route to coordination
Conway’s law applies only to software and has no bearing on hospitals
It wrongly assumes the electronic record is fragmented
Service-line structures cannot exist in hospitals

questions.explanation: The review of 142 studies found mirroring common but not universal, with major exceptions where coordination ran through shared code, documentation and tools. The argument turns a tendency into a guarantee and then discards exactly the mechanism—shared standards—that the evidence shows can do the integrating work. Reorganizing may help, but it is neither necessary nor sufficient.

optionFeedback.b: The mirroring idea has been studied well beyond software and is a reasonable diagnostic for any designed system, including records and processes.
optionFeedback.c: The fragmentation is stipulated in the scenario; the flaw is in the causal reasoning, not the premise.
optionFeedback.d: Service lines are a common hospital structure; nothing in the argument depends on their being impossible.

questions.prompt: Which assessment of this fictional study is most accurate?

stimulus.text: Fictional study. Researchers interviewed managers at 400 outpatient clinics using a double-blind structured interview and scored management practices from 1 to 5. Clinics in the top quarter of management scores had, on average, 12 percent shorter patient wait times and 8 percent higher patient satisfaction than clinics in the bottom quarter. Top-quarter clinics were also more likely to belong to large health systems and to be located in metropolitan areas. The authors conclude: “Adopting structured management practices will shorten wait times by about 12 percent.”

options.text: The conclusion is justified because the interviews were double-blind
The association is informative, but the causal conclusion is not justified: system membership and location may drive both scores and wait times, and no practices were assigned
The study shows no relationship, because satisfaction is a subjective measure
The conclusion is justified because 400 clinics is a large sample

questions.explanation: Double-blind interviewing protects the measurement of practices, but it does nothing about confounding. Clinics in large metropolitan systems may have better practices and shorter waits for the same underlying reasons, such as resources and staffing. The study supports an association; estimating the effect of adopting practices requires assigning them, as the textile experiment did, or a credible quasi-experiment.

optionFeedback.a: Blinding reduces measurement bias; it cannot remove confounding by system membership or location.
optionFeedback.c: Wait times are an objective measure, and a subjective outcome can still be informative; the problem is causal inference, not measurement type.
optionFeedback.d: Sample size reduces random error, not bias from confounding; a large confounded study is precisely wrong.

questions.prompt: A software company rewards engineers mainly on the number of tickets closed per sprint, and complaints about quality are rising. Which changes are consistent with the multitask model and with sound practice against Goodhart’s law? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pair ticket counts with measures of reopened tickets and customer-reported defects
Raise the bonus per ticket so engineers work harder overall
Reduce the weight of ticket counts in pay and add periodic peer review of code quality
Give hard-to-measure architecture work to a role evaluated on it rather than on tickets
Stop measuring anything, because every measure will be gamed
Audit a random sample of closed tickets each month to check that the work was done well

questions.explanation: The multitask model recommends weaker incentives on the measurable task when important work is hard to measure, grouping hard-to-measure work into roles evaluated on it, and adding measures or reviews that capture neglected dimensions. Auditing and pairing measures protect against Goodhart-style gaming. Raising the bonus strengthens the distortion, and abandoning measurement leaves gaming invisible rather than absent.

optionFeedback.a: Correct: a paired counter-measure reveals quality lost to speed.
optionFeedback.b: A larger bonus on the measured task pulls even more effort away from unmeasured quality.
optionFeedback.c: Correct: weaker incentives plus judgment-based review is the model’s central remedy.
optionFeedback.d: Correct: job design that groups hard-to-measure work is one of the model’s implications.
optionFeedback.e: Goodhart’s law argues for protecting measures, not abandoning them; without measures, gaming continues unseen.
optionFeedback.f: Correct: periodic audit checks the reality behind the number.

questions.prompt: Rank these sources of evidence for the claim that structured management practices *cause* higher productivity, from strongest to weakest.

options.text: A survey finding that firms with higher management scores are more productive
A randomized experiment in which plants chosen at random get help adopting practices and are compared with control plants
A consultant’s account of three client turnarounds after introducing practices
A before-and-after comparison of plants that adopted practices against similar plants that did not over the same period

questions.explanation: Random assignment gives the strongest causal evidence because it balances confounders on average. A before-and-after comparison with a matched comparison group removes stable differences between plants and common shocks, though not differences in why plants chose to adopt. A cross-sectional survey shows association but cannot rule out reverse causation. Three selected success stories are the weakest: no comparison, and cases are chosen because they succeeded.

optionFeedback.a: A survey is informative about association but cannot separate cause from selection; it ranks below designs with comparison over time.
optionFeedback.c: Selected success stories lack any comparison group and suffer from survivorship; they rank last.
optionFeedback.d: A comparison-group design over time is strong but still vulnerable to self-selection into adoption, so it ranks below randomization.

questions.prompt: Using Hackman’s conditions, select every real design problem in this team charter.

stimulus.text: Charter — Patient Flow Improvement Team (fictional hospital). Purpose: “Make things better for patients.” Members: whoever is free from the ten wards that week. Decision authority: recommendations go to the Patient Flow Steering Committee, which meets twice a year. Data: the team may request data from the analytics department; requests are handled after other work. Rewards: members are evaluated only by their home ward managers, on ward measures. Coaching: the sponsoring vice president will attend the launch meeting. Norms: none recorded.

options.text: Membership is unbounded and changes weekly, so it is not a real team
The purpose is too vague to provide a compelling direction
The team is too small to be effective
Recommendations wait months for a decision, so the team cannot see or learn from the results of its work
Rewards and data access do not support team work, so the organizational context undermines the team
The sponsor’s attendance at the launch meeting provides the coaching the team needs
No norms of conduct are recorded, which weakens the team’s structure

questions.explanation: The charter fails nearly every condition: no stable, bounded membership (not a real team), a vague purpose (no compelling direction), no norms (weak enabling structure), slow decision outlets plus rewards and data that ignore team work (unsupportive context). One appearance at a launch is not coaching. Team size is not stated, so it cannot be identified as a problem.

optionFeedback.a: Correct: shifting, unbounded membership fails the first condition.
optionFeedback.b: Correct: a slogan is not a clear, challenging, consequential purpose.
optionFeedback.c: The charter does not state a size; inventing a problem the document does not show is a common issue-spotting error.
optionFeedback.d: Correct: a twice-yearly decision outlet cuts the team off from the consequences of its work.
optionFeedback.e: Correct: evaluation on ward measures and last-in-line data access signal that the organization does not support the team.
optionFeedback.f: A single launch appearance is not ongoing, competent help with how the team works.
optionFeedback.g: Correct: explicit norms of conduct are part of an enabling structure.

questions.prompt: In 120–180 words, explain why a well-designed reorganization can still lower performance for a period, using the concept of organizational routines. Then propose two specific ways to reduce that cost. (Self-assessed against the rubric and model answer.)
questions.modelAnswer: Routines are the regular patterns of coordinated activity through which an organization does its work. Much of the knowledge they carry is tacit—who to call about an exception, which hand-offs need checking—and routines also act as a truce that settles who does what. A reorganization changes reporting lines and roles, which breaks hand-offs and reopens the truce. Even if the new structure fits the work better, people must rebuild coordination and rediscover tacit knowledge, so performance can dip until new routines form. Two ways to reduce the cost: first, map the few critical routines and hand-offs before the change—by watching them run, not only by asking—and assign an owner to carry each one across the transition. Second, sequence the change: move the parts with the weakest routines first, keep experienced people in place through at least one full cycle of the work, and pair newcomers with them so tacit knowledge transfers.

rubric.criterion: Explains the mechanism: routines store tacit knowledge and settle conflicts, so reorganizing disrupts them
levels: 0 — mechanism missing or reduced to “people resist change”
1 — mentions routines but not why disruption costs performance
2 — clear account of tacit knowledge and the truce, and why rebuilding takes time

rubric.criterion: Proposes two specific, workable mitigations tied to the mechanism
levels: 1 — one specific mitigation, or two loosely tied to routines
2 — two specific mitigations that protect or transfer routines

questions.prompt: About nine years after the Indian textile experiment, researchers found that roughly half the adopted practices had been dropped. Among the reasons most often given were managerial turnover and a lack of directors’ time. What does this most directly suggest for a leader introducing new practices?

options.text: The practices were never really effective, so the original experiment was wrong
Practices last only if they are carried by people and routines that survive turnover, so embedding them deserves explicit attention
Practices decay at a fixed rate regardless of what managers do
Only external consultants can sustain management practices

questions.explanation: The follow-up still found a large gap between treated and control plants, so the practices mattered; but they decayed where the people who carried them left or lacked time. That is the routine argument in practice: a practice becomes durable when it is embedded in roles, cadences and hand-offs that do not depend on one person.

optionFeedback.a: The lasting gap between treated and control plants indicates the practices had real effects; partial decay is not evidence that they never worked.
optionFeedback.c: The reasons given—turnover and directors’ time—point to causes leaders can influence, not a fixed rate.
optionFeedback.d: Practices spread within firms to plants that never had consultants, which shows that people inside firms can sustain them.

reserve.prompt: A large law firm coordinates most of its work through the years of training and professional certification its lawyers share, so that partners and associates can work together with little supervision. Which configuration and coordinating mechanism does this describe?

options.text: Professional bureaucracy; standardization of skills
Machine bureaucracy; standardization of work processes
Adhocracy; mutual adjustment
Simple structure; direct supervision

reserve.explanation: When professionals coordinate largely because shared training tells each what to expect of the others, Mintzberg calls the mechanism standardization of skills and the configuration a professional bureaucracy. Hospitals and universities are the other classic examples.

optionFeedback.b: A machine bureaucracy specifies the work method itself, as in claims processing; professionals resist that kind of scripting.
optionFeedback.c: An adhocracy coordinates through informal, continuous adjustment in project teams, not mainly through prior training.
optionFeedback.d: Direct supervision by one person cannot coordinate a large professional firm.

reserve.prompt: Which allocation of pricing decisions best fits Jensen and Meckling’s logic?

stimulus.text: A hypothetical hotel chain sets room prices with a central revenue system that sees bookings, competitor rates and seasonality across the chain. Local general managers know about events the system misses—a conference moving to town, a road closure, a rival hotel’s renovation. General managers are paid a bonus on occupancy, which they can raise by cutting prices.

options.text: Centralize all pricing in the revenue system and ignore local input
Give general managers full authority over prices, since they hold the local knowledge
Let the central system set prices, allow general managers to adjust within a band for documented local events, and pair the occupancy bonus with a revenue-per-room measure
Rotate pricing authority monthly between the central team and the general managers

reserve.explanation: Local event knowledge is specific and valuable, so some decision rights should move toward it; but the occupancy bonus gives general managers a reason to underprice, an agency cost. The banded right captures the knowledge while limiting the damage, and pairing occupancy with revenue per room aligns the measure with the chain’s interest—decision rights, measurement and rewards designed together.

optionFeedback.a: Full centralization wastes specific local knowledge that the system cannot capture cheaply.
optionFeedback.b: Full delegation ignores the agency cost created by an occupancy-only bonus.
optionFeedback.d: Rotation creates inconsistency without addressing either the knowledge or the incentive problem.

reserve.prompt: A hospital is rewarded for reducing the share of emergency patients who wait more than four hours. The share falls sharply, but staff report that patients are moved to a hallway “assessment area” at about three hours and fifty minutes, where they continue to wait. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Goodhart’s law: the measure became a target and is being moved without improving the outcome it tracked
The measure was invalid from the start and should never have been used
Regression to the mean after an unusually bad period
Evidence that structured management practices do not work in hospitals

reserve.explanation: The number improved because its definition was met, not because patients were treated sooner—the signature of a measure turned target. The response is to pair the measure with one that captures the real outcome (total time to treatment) and to audit what happens near the threshold, not to abandon measurement.

optionFeedback.b: The measure was a reasonable indicator before it carried rewards; gaming does not prove it was invalid as a measure.
optionFeedback.c: Regression to the mean would not produce a cluster of transfers just before the threshold.
optionFeedback.d: One gamed target is not evidence against monitoring and targets in general; it is evidence that targets need protection.

reserve.prompt: Which statement best summarizes Hackman’s view of how leaders contribute to team performance?

options.text: Mostly through their personal style in meetings and conversations
Mostly by designing and supporting the conditions under which a team can manage itself
Hardly at all, because team composition determines everything
Mostly through individual incentives they offer each member

reserve.explanation: Hackman argued that a leader’s main contribution lies in creating the conditions—a real team, compelling direction, enabling structure, supportive context and coaching—rather than in interpersonal style. Composition is part of an enabling structure, not the whole story, and individual incentives can undercut collective work.

optionFeedback.a: Style matters less, in Hackman’s account, than the conditions a leader designs.
optionFeedback.c: Composition is one element of an enabling structure; Hackman gives leaders a large role through design.
optionFeedback.d: Individual incentives can work against a team’s collective output; a supportive context rewards team results.

assignment.title: Design a Department

brief.text: Design a department you could defend to a skeptical executive committee. You may choose a fictional player development or baseball operations department—kept generic, with an invented organization and no real club, staff or proprietary practice—or a department in another field you know or want to understand: a hospital service, a fintech risk unit, a public agency office, a consulting practice. The domain matters less than the design reasoning.

Make the trade-offs explicit. A strong design names what the department will do badly or not at all, and why that is the right price for what it does well. Use the week’s frameworks by name where they inform a choice: differentiation and integration, Galbraith’s strategies, Mintzberg’s mechanisms, span arithmetic, Jensen and Meckling’s knowledge-and-agency trade-off, a labelled practitioner tool for decision rights, the multitask model and Hackman’s conditions.

items: State a fixed annual staff budget of your choosing, and keep the design within it.
Include at least one recurring decision that crosses into another department.
Include at least one important task that is hard to measure, and say who protects it.
Make every name, number and organization fictional, and label numbers as synthetic.

brief.text: You may build the structure in the Organization Builder first and describe the result here. The Builder’s checks are a useful audit of arithmetic, spans and coverage; they do not evaluate your reasoning, and your design may knowingly fail a check if you explain why.

assignment.deliverable: A department design document of 1,200–1,800 words, with an organization chart as an indented list, a decision-rights table and a metrics table.

template.heading: Mandate and boundaries
template.guidance: In 100–150 words: what the department exists to do, for whom, and what it explicitly does not do. Name the main uncertainty it faces and the clock (or clocks) its work runs on.

template.heading: Structure and reporting lines
template.guidance: An indented organization chart with spans and layers. Name the coordinating mechanism that does most of the work and explain why this structure fits the uncertainty you named.

template.heading: Roles and staffing
template.guidance: For each role: purpose, core skills, synthetic cost and the work it owns. Show the total against your budget and identify any single points of failure.

template.heading: Decision rights
template.guidance: A table of 5–8 recurring decisions with Recommend, Input, Agree (if any), Decide and Informed—labelled as a practitioner heuristic. For two decisions, explain where the specific knowledge sits and how you contain agency costs.

template.heading: Coordination mechanisms and operating rhythm
template.guidance: The integrating devices you rely on (roles, routines, information systems, slack) and the meeting cadence—daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly—with what each meeting decides and who attends.

template.heading: Metrics and incentives
template.guidance: Four to six measures and what each is for. For each measure tied to evaluation, name the cheapest way to game it and your countermeasure. Identify the important work that is hard to measure and who protects it.

template.heading: Trade-offs accepted and redesign triggers
template.guidance: The two or three trade-offs you chose deliberately, what you gave up, and the observable signals that would make you redesign within a year.

rubric.criterion: Fit between mandate, work and structure

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: The structure follows visibly from the mandate and the uncertainty of the work; differentiation is deliberate and matched by named integrating mechanisms; spans and layers are justified with arithmetic.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: The structure is plausible for the mandate, and most choices are justified; one or two links between uncertainty and structure are asserted rather than argued.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: A reasonable chart, but the reasons are generic; differentiation or integration is not addressed explicitly.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: The chart does not follow from the mandate, or the structure is copied without diagnosis.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Every listed decision has exactly one Decide holder; vetoes are limited to genuine constraints; two decisions are analyzed in terms of specific knowledge and agency costs, with the control system that contains them.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Decision ownership is clear and mostly well placed; the knowledge-and-agency analysis is present but thin for one decision.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Decisions are listed but ownership is ambiguous in places, or the tool is used without reasoning about knowledge or incentives.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Decision rights are missing, contradictory or assigned without explanation.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Integrating devices target the specific coordination problems identified; the cadence matches the work’s clocks; each meeting has a defined question, inputs and decision rights; routines that carry knowledge are protected.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: A sensible cadence and mechanisms, with minor gaps in what some meetings decide or how hand-offs work.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Meetings are listed without clear purposes, or mechanisms are named without linking them to coordination problems.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No coherent account of how the department coordinates or reviews its work.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Measures map to the mandate; each evaluative measure has a named gaming risk and a countermeasure; hard-to-measure work is identified and protected using multitask logic.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Good measures with countermeasures for most; protection of hard-to-measure work is present but general.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Measures are listed without gaming analysis, or incentives are strong on easily gamed measures.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Measures are missing, unrelated to the mandate, or certain to be gamed.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Trade-offs are explicit and owned; claims are labelled as research, practitioner heuristic or the author’s judgment; redesign triggers are observable; all details are fictional and synthetic.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Trade-offs are named and mostly justified; evidence labels are present with minor lapses.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Trade-offs are implied rather than stated; heuristics are presented as findings in places.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No trade-offs acknowledged, or the design relies on unlabelled claims or non-fictional details.

prompts: Think of the last time a decision in your organization stalled or was made twice. Who held the decision right on paper, who held it in practice, and who held the knowledge it needed? What one change would have helped?
Which measure that you report, or are judged on, has drifted furthest from the outcome it was meant to track? What would you pair it with?
Name one routine you personally carry that would weaken if you were away for three months. What would it take to make it independent of you, and is that worth the effort?
Where in your own work would you choose slack over another coordinating mechanism, and how would you defend that choice to a finance colleague who sees only the idle cost?

review.front: What are differentiation and integration, and what did Lawrence and Lorsch find about effective organizations?
review.back: Differentiation is how far subunits diverge in goals, time horizons, interpersonal style and formality; integration is the collaboration that reconnects them. Effective organizations achieved both in the degree their environment demanded—not the least differentiation.

review.front: Galbraith: what are the two families of response when task uncertainty overloads the hierarchy?
review.back: Reduce the need for information processing (slack resources, self-contained units) or increase capacity to process it (vertical information systems, lateral relations). Each has a cost; choosing none means lower performance.
Direct supervision; standardization of work processes; standardization of outputs; standardization of skills; mutual adjustment.

review.front: For 1,000 frontline staff, what happens to layers and total managers when the average span rises from 5 to 12?
review.back: Layers fall from 5 to 3 and managers from 251 to 92 (synthetic arithmetic). The saving also removes exception-handling and coaching capacity.

review.front: Why is “fit” a risky concept in contingency theory?
review.back: If fit is defined after the fact as whatever successful organizations did, the theory cannot fail. A testable claim defines required fit in advance from measurable features of the task.

review.front: Specific versus general knowledge—why does the difference matter for decision rights?
review.back: Specific knowledge is costly to transmit, so decisions using it are better made where it sits; general knowledge is cheap to move, so those decisions can be centralized.

review.front: Jensen and Meckling: which three systems make up an organization’s structure?
review.back: The assignment of decision rights, the system for measuring performance, and the system for rewarding and punishing. They must be designed together.

review.front: Five signals for sorting decisions between center and periphery?
review.back: Where the knowledge sits; the cost of inconsistency; the speed required; interdependence with other units; whether local interests are aligned.

review.front: What does the evidence say about Conway’s law?
review.back: A review of 142 studies found mirroring between organization and product structure common but not universal; open collaborative projects coordinating through shared tools were the main exception.

review.front: How did Bloom and Van Reenen measure management, and what did they find?
review.back: Double-blind interviews scoring practices in monitoring, targets and people management (732 firms, four countries). Scores varied widely and went with productivity, profitability, market value and survival.

review.front: What did the Indian textile experiment and its follow-up show?
review.back: Randomly chosen plants given consulting raised productivity 17% in the first year (published estimate). About nine years later, roughly half the practices had been dropped, yet a significant gap remained.

review.front: State Goodhart’s law and its mechanism.
review.back: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure: people find the cheapest ways to move the number, which often do not improve the underlying outcome.

review.front: Holmström and Milgrom’s multitask model: what does it predict and recommend?
review.back: Strong incentives on measurable tasks pull effort from hard-to-measure ones. Remedies: weaker incentives, grouping tasks by measurability, and roles evaluated on the neglected work.

review.front: What should each layer of an operating rhythm answer?
review.back: Daily: what is blocked today? Weekly: are we on track? Monthly: are outcomes moving and are measures honest? Quarterly: are we doing the right work? (Practitioner design.)

review.front: Why do routines make organizations both reliable and slow to change?
review.back: Routines store tacit operational knowledge and settle who does what (a truce). Changing them reopens the truce and discards unwritten knowledge.

review.front: Hackman’s five conditions for team effectiveness?
review.back: A real team, a compelling direction, an enabling structure, a supportive organizational context, and expert coaching—conditions matter more than leader style.

preview.text: Week 9 turns from how an organization is built to what it is built for: strategy, capabilities and competitive advantage, where routines return as the source of capabilities that rivals find hard to copy. Week 10 puts prices on the choices you made here, from headcount to the cost of slack. Week 12 returns to operating rhythms, dashboards and leading versus lagging indicators when strategy has to become execution. Week 13 revisits decision rights and incentives as questions of governance and accountability. The Week 14 capstone asks you to design a department’s structure, staffing model and decision rights, using the Organization Builder you met this week.

links.why: Routines and organizational capabilities as sources of competitive advantage.
Costing personnel, slack and structural choices.
Operating rhythms, dashboards and leading versus lagging indicators in implementation.
Decision rights, incentives and principal–agent problems as governance questions.
The capstone’s organizational structure, staffing model and decision-rights components.
